image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Side-by-side **stacked vertical bar chart** (timeline-style comparison of transit times).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **stacking** within each vertical bar to show component durations.
   - Uses a **side-by-side comparison** of two bars: “Typically 59 days” vs. “Currently 87 days.”
   - Includes **annotation callouts** and **icons** to explain delays and transportation modes.
   - No faceting or small multiples beyond the two compared bars.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario (“Typically” vs. “Currently”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate side-by-side bars; top labels |
| Total transit time (days) | Quantitative | Overall bar height; top text labels (“59 days”, “87 days”) |
| Transit stage duration (days for each segment) | Quantitative | Height of stacked bar segments; numeric labels inside segments |
| Transit stage / shipment milestone (e.g., cargo ready to depart Indonesia, arrival in Vancouver, arrival in Ferndale, arrival in Orlando) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical position of orange milestone dots; text labels/callouts |
| Transportation mode | Categorical/nominal | Icons (factory/ship/rail/truck) placed alongside the bar; associated segment position |
| Delay explanation / cause | Categorical/nominal (textual annotation) | Annotation text connected by dotted leader lines |
| Sequence/order of shipment journey | Ordinal | Vertical ordering from top to bottom along the bars |

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that compared to the typical 59 days for usual cargo transportation, in the present day it is almost a month longer for the same process we used to practice. It is clear that the graphs are used to compare the length of time needed to transmit cargo from Indonesia to Orlando, Florida through the title of the comparison. I believe it is longer because of the social issues like the pandemic causing many workers to stay home due to fear of getting sick. In general, many of the processes like the lead times and times needed to anchor in the seas have been extended likely due to the lack of staff. This affects me and my community because, with longer wait times, we'll have to wait longer for certain goods that we utilize on a daily basis. We might have to wait weeks or even months just for a single product we like from a specific company as a result of these delays. I believe that with this information I can come up with the headline "The Cargo Can't Wait to Travel! Or Maybe It's Waiting too Much?", which uses satire and humor in order to attract an audience to educate them on why shipments are taking longer than usual.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed right away the drastic difference in length between the two flow charts showing cargo transit times. I also noticed that the length of the transportation mode of the current transit time is 53 days, almost as long as the 59 days typical transit time total. I also saw many people complaining on TikTok that parts of their costumes were delayed, so it seems to be a common issue affecting many people. Based on this, a catchy title for this graph could be, "Increased Transit Times Resulting in Consumer Delivery Delays".

This depends on what cargo is being imported. If we can't import raw materials fast enough, I think shortages in certain products could be likely since we can't manufacture them soon enough. My title for this graph is "Transit Delays: Why are they Increasing?"

1. I noticed that limits in the amount of products ships can hold is delaying lead times. Along with limited capacity, extra anchorage time also leads to delayed shipping and transport times, as it causes port congestion. For example, before arriving in Orlando it can take up to 60 days for the whole transport and departure process to take place. 
2. I wonder if the long and extra port congestion will have an impact on the environment of ports. Port waters are already filled with boats unloading cargo, and delayed departures from ports leads to more fuel and gas being deposited into the bodies of water around these ports. This not only pollutes the water but endangers aquatic life and the ecosystem of that body of water. 
3. This relates to me and my community because as global trade becomes more popular and easier, people are more likely to buy international goods. This means increased shipments and ships in port waters because of limited capacity and increased product demand. More ships in ports means a longer delay in ports and more pollution in the body of water. Many people demand fast shipping but don't realize the larger negative impacts it has on our environment. 
4. Title: "Snail Shipping"

comments.raw_comment: This graph shows the increase in cargo transit times from Indonesia to Orlando, Fla. in recent days. Many Americans are facing a very large increase in the cost of goods but also a very large increase in the shipping time for goods. This is because, as shown in the graph, the cargo ports and warehouses are so congested from the surplus shipping of goods that it is putting a delay on all goods. I notice that typical transit times from Indonesia to Orlando, Fla. is 59 days, but now it takes 87 days. That is a huge increase in time for goods to ship and so I wonder what it is going to take to fix this. I also think that during the holiday season, this time is just going to continue to increase because now everyone has to buy gifts. I wonder when things are going to get better and if they are, how are people going to fix it.  The biggest reason for this is Coronavirus. This virus has changed every dynamic in the world. Everyone is ordering items online rather than going out to buy them because they don't need to be in contact with people online. This affects me and my community because I have experienced shipping delays in the past few months/year. I have ordered items online and when they normally ship in 1-2 weeks, they have shipped a month. This is affecting everyone in the world and I hope that it gets better soon. A catchy headline is, "Stuffed to the Brim".

1. What do you notice?
Storage capacity limits are skyrocketing because of more and more shopping online and the demand for products has increased over the past couple of years. Among human delays, wildfires and other natural disasters extend the time of transit for a product to reach its destination.
2. What do you wonder?
Is there an easier/faster solution to prevent congestion at transportation sites across the globe? If so what would it cost and is it within reach/feasible?
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
Holiday shopping shipping times have increased preventing gifts from reaching their destination before their hopeful arrival. I work at Target and the recent delays have increased working hours for most of the employees as more products are being purchased through the stores’ online distribution option. Before COVID the impact this had on staff was minimal but now that COVID has prevented some individuals from shopping inside the store the demand for online orders has increased exponentially.
4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
People arent the alone in congestion...the global trade is too.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
The very first thing I notice is the header at the top of the graph distinguishing that the graph is discussing cargo transit times from Indonesia to Florida. After this, I make the connection that it takes a lot of time to make this journey when there are multiple stops taken. It can normally be a two day trip, but with the ships stopping in various places it takes ample more time. 
What do you wonder?
I have never seen this type of graph before and I wonder what it is called and what its main use is. I also wonder if there are people on the transit ships when they are making the additional stops. Is it cheaper to go on a ship that takes a longer period of time sort of like an airplane with layovers?
How does this relate to you and your community?
This does not directly relate to me and my community, but rather by an extension. These cargo ships are carrying items my household may have ordered, and with the additional stops it takes longer for my package to arrive. 
Create a headline. 
"Shipping...Shipping...Shipping... purchase your holiday items NOW"

comments.raw_comment:
1.) I noticed that there is a drastic change in terms of the the typical transit time. More specifically, it typically takes 59 days to transit from Indonesia to Orlando. However, there is an 18 day difference if we were to fast forward to currently. This is due to the fact that capacity limits are creating longer lead times, along with extra anchorage time. Additionally, warehouses are full, so therefore its harder to encounter facilities with free space. Overall, the time to ship and transit has dramatically increased, leaving me with various questions along with concern. 
2.) I wonder what implications this might have on the American consumer population, especially with the holiday season right around the corner. I also wonder if this has any specific relation to Covid-19. Maybe overconsumption?
3.) In my community, most people shop online. On a daily basis, I think I see at least 20 delivery trucks pass my house, deliver packages to neighbors, or enter the main road. With shipping and transit times being consistently increased, this may breed frustration in my neighborhood, specifically because we are so reliant on online shopping. Not only in the online sense, my family as well as those who live around me shop a lot. I consistently see neighbors unloading bags of goodies, emphasizing the detrimental impact these delays have on my community. 
4.) Shipping delays? The Ultimate Pain!

comments.raw_comment: This graph showcases the supply chain delays that the supply and demand have caused. I believe it is comparing and contrasting two different cargo times traveling from Indonesia to Florida. One cargo time took 59 days to get to Florida and the other took 87 days. It took the second cargo an extra ten days to be ready to depart Indonesia. In addition, traveling time was an extra 15 days compared to the first cargo. Overall, many of the delays seem to be because there's too many goods for the current state of things like warehouses and ports. The supply was no ready for the amount of demand. I think a good name for the graph would be, "Cargo transit times vary in reponse to supply chain crisis"

Another thing I wonder is why it takes so long to get from Vancouver to Washington, when they are right next to each other. It might be an issue with crossing national borders though. I would imagine that it would already take that long to go down the West Coast and through Central America. 

This affects me and my community because supply chain delays result in my purchased goods taking longer time to get to my house.

comments.raw_comment:
This graph shows that the cargo transit times from Indonesia to Orlando, Florida have become longer. I noticed that it now takes a longer time to ship goods from Indonesia to Orlando Florida. The transportation time for the goods had increased from 59 days to 87 days. This is due to port congestion, extra anchorage time and terminal congestion. The boat traveling time has increased from 38 days to 53 days.  Cargo preparation in Indonesia now takes 18 days while before it only took 8 days. I wonder what is causing these shipping delays.  I think it may be due to the shortage of workers in the shipping industries.  Also many deliveries are behind which is causing port congestion. I also wonder if the coronavirus pandemic affected the shipping deliveries. Are there less workers and delays in the shipping industry due to the coronavirus pandemic? 1. What do you notice?

It is taking significantly longer for cargo to get from Indonesia to Florida. A whole extra 10 days in warehouses and 15 days in transportation!

This relates to me and my community because some places have not had as much items in stock as they usually do. This should be an accurate time estimate from Indonesia to Long Island, NY as well because it is on the water as Florida is.

Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s flowchart shows the supply chain delays that are producing consumer goods and inventory shortages, long delivery delays and price increases -- inflation.   What factors contribute to these delays and how long will they affect inflation and the employment rate?  And, will you be getting a back-order slip in your Christmas stocking or as a holiday gift?

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to the four questions in the release.  By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, Nov. 19 with moderation on Wednesday, Dec. 1.  The topic:  global carbon displayed on a treemap graph.  Keep noticing and wondering!

We notice that there are delays in the current cargo transit from Indonesia to Orlando Florida. This is because there is a lot of congestion at the ports. There is a lot of supply but not enough demand for these product.

Both horizontal axis demonstrate this idea with the typical transit time and the actual transit time. There are labels with the number of days at certain points of the transportation. Something that is interesting is that global events affect congestion in ports, which in turn increases the time it takes for goods to be transported.

One thing we wonder is how the pandemic has affected this. Not only that, but we wonder if the ship that blocked the Suez canal had lasting effects that still effect the current time shown in this graph. One final aspect of this graph that we wonder about is whether the location of the destination and departure, Indonesia and Florida, affects certain factors like which canals the shipping container goes through, weather over the ocean, and the route that the ship takes.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that the cargo times from Indonesia to Orlando, Florida have increased by 28 days. Specifically the times from Indonesia to Vancouver, British Columbia significantly increased to 15 days. Additionally, getting the cargo ready to depart Indonesia increased by 10. I wonder how and why the capacity limits changed in Indonesia since it is impacting the lead times to be longer. Additionally, I wonder when porting congestion and extra anchorage started to occur because it has impacted the departure and arrival times to increase significantly. I wonder what they are doing to reduce the cargo transit times and resolve the issue like using planning, a better outsourcing model, and stronger scheduling. This relates to me and my community because there is an ongoing trend with economic outsourcing especially online. An abundance of people ranging from adolescents to adults order a lot of things online. While ordering online, there is a long delayment in shipping packages out and obtaining our deliveries. We figured out a portion of why sometimes things don't come in on time and why things outside the country take a long time to ship. The graph demonstrates how a larger population and increase in supply and demand impacts outsourcing in the cargo transit times from Indonesia to Orlando, Florida; additionally, it may impact future production and outsourcing which can cause distress. A catchy headline to wrap the main idea is, "Products Placed in Postponement!"
